title: PolarisComms - reserved GPU + VPC burst intake
summary: Intro discovery to understand PolarisComms' inference peaks for real-time personalization, discussing tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated vs private; focus on reserved GPUs, VPC network isolation, warm-pool burst handling and compliance needs. Agreed next steps: Redwood to provide initial sizing spreadsheet, security pack, and schedule a short benchmarking window for a 24h peak simulation.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-01-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Leo Martinez (Redwood SE) — Maya Patel (PolarisComms Head of Platform), Owen Li (SRE), Nora Chen (ML Eng), Samir Vyas (Security)

Optional auto-sections:
Action items and POC notes sprinkled through the transcript.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Kim (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time, um we'll kick off, i'm jordan from redwood inference, ae on the account, and priya and leo are engineering, priya will drive most of the technical Qs.
[00:12] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): hi thanks, all good on our side, quick background — we run personalization for live sports streaming, so bursts around game starts are huge, short windows, latency matters a lot.
[00:24] Priya Nair (Redwood): love that — so the core ask is predictable capacity during peaks and isolation for customer data, is that right?
[00:30] Owen Li (PolarisComms): yep, and we have to keep tail latency under 120ms P95 for personalized snippets; currently using a mix — in-house k8s endpoints for smaller models and a hosted provider for burst but it's getting expensive and not consistent.
[00:44] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): also want to avoid noisy neighbor issues at peak — we've had token throttles mid-game which is, uh, bad for product.
[00:52] Leo Martinez (Redwood): totally, that's exactly where dedicated reserved GPUs help, you get a predictable baseline and then options for warm pool or burst to cloud-hosted variants — we can also route per policy to fallbacks.
[01:03] Samir Vyas (PolarisComms): security first — we need SOC2, KMS for key management, SSO/SAML, and VPC peering or on-prem option for certain PII flows. What's typical for folks wanting isolation?
[01:16] Priya Nair (Redwood): most enterprise customers pick Dedicated for the steady-state with VPC peering and private networking. For the most regulated flows they keep a Private deployment or on-prem path. Our private offering supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. For SOC2 we can share our certs and pen test reports — we'll send the pack.
[01:33] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): good — send that. Can you explain warm pools vs reserved nodes? Are warm pools prewarmed GPUs or just prewarmed containers?
[01:45] Jordan Kim (Redwood): short answer: warm pools are reserved compute that's kept ready to accept new requests (preloaded weights and KV caches), reserved nodes are your committed capacity. Warm pools can be configured as part of your Dedicated contract for fast ramp. There's also hot-pool sticky behavior — we can keep certain models hot to reduce cold-start tail.
[02:04] Owen Li (PolarisComms): how fast do warm pools spin up, say we need 5x our baseline for 90 seconds at kickoff?
[02:11] Priya Nair (Redwood): depends on topology, model size and whether the KV cache can be shared. For 5x 90s spikes, most customers size a small warm pool to cover the first wave and then allow autoscaling with burst contracts. Historically we see warm-pool activation within 10-25s for medium models if weights are resident; full KV warming maybe another 30s.
[02:36] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): hmm — that might still be long for our use case. We do a 10-15s window at kickoff where latency must be low. Is there a pattern to keep a minimal hot set always resident?
[02:49] Leo Martinez (Redwood): yes — model pinning. You can pin the small personalization micro-models to a hot pool. Then for larger generative models we use autoscaling and fallback. That gives you sub-50ms token latency because the micro-models are memory-resident.
[03:06] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): what's the billing model for warm pool minutes? Do we pay for reserved capacity only or also for prewarm minutes?
[03:13] Jordan Kim (Redwood): reserved commit covers the capacity; warm-pool minutes are typically billed as part of a burst add-on or included depending on contract tier. We'll include cost modeling in the sizing sheet.
[03:24] Owen Li (PolarisComms): on the fallback side — if dedicated capacity is exhausted during a massive surge, can we failover to a hosted model with a graceful degradation for non-sensitive requests?
[03:35] Priya Nair (Redwood): yes, smart routing policies can route by region, latency tolerance, or data sensitivity. You can set rules like: route PII requests to Private/Dedicated only; everything else may use hosted fallback with model variant that is cheaper. We also maintain per-route SLOs and can do circuit-breakers.
[03:55] Samir Vyas (PolarisComms): and audit logs for routed requests? We require per-request traceability for audits.
[04:01] Priya Nair (Redwood): audit logs and tracing are available in Redwood Console; token-level traces, model version, route, and latency are recorded. We can export logs to your SIEM via S3 or streaming.
[04:12] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): quick technical: we use quantized 4-bit models for edge but have larger FP16 variants for quality. Does Redwood support multiple quantization artifacts per model and automatic fallback?
[04:24] Leo Martinez (Redwood): yes, we support multiple model variants and quantization profiles. The runtime can serve quantized variants and fall back to higher-precision models if the lower-precision quality drifts. We also have quality monitoring tied to prompt sets so you can detect regression.
[04:40] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): interesting — we also want preemptible spot for lower priority workloads to save cost. Can we mix spot nodes for non-critical tasks?
[04:50] Jordan Kim (Redwood): absolutely — you can designate capacity pools with cost tiers: spot/backfill for async batch, dedicated reserved for low-latency requests. Our scheduler respects eviction tolerance policies.
[04:59] Owen Li (PolarisComms): networking: we need VPC peering and strict egress controls; can we use customer-managed NAT and have no public egress from inference nodes?
[05:09] Priya Nair (Redwood): yes, VPC peering or private link; we support egress controls and you can place a NAT gateway or egress proxy on your side. Private deployments give you even more control for air-gapped flows.
[05:20] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): timeline and decision criteria — we're aiming to run a pilot for Q2 and go-live fall. Our success criteria: stable latency under 120ms P95 across kickoff spikes, cost per 1000 requests under our current baseline, and SOC2 plus KMS integration.
[05:34] Jordan Kim (Redwood): that sounds reasonable. Next we should get telemetry from you — historical QPS, spike multipliers, model sizes, and token lengths. We'll produce a sizing recommendation.
[05:45] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): we have telemetry — average 120 RPS baseline, spikes to 900 RPS for 90-180s after kickoff, tokens per request avg 64, max bursts include longer sequences but rare.
[05:58] Leo Martinez (Redwood): got it — rough nudge: to cover 900 RPS at low latency you need N reserved GPUs depending on model, but we'll run an exact calc. Do you run batching now?
[06:08] Owen Li (PolarisComms): yes, we batch to 16 on in-house endpoints, but it's brittle, we want Redwood to manage batching and kv cache.
[06:16] Priya Nair (Redwood): our runtime will manage continuous batching and KV cache; we can also recommend batch size and concurrency for your latency goals.
[06:24] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): compliance: Samir wants to confirm KMS integration and whether keys can be customer-created in their cloud KMS.
[06:32] Samir Vyas (PolarisComms): yes, we must retain control of encryption keys for PII payloads, prefer to avoid key escrow.
[06:39] Priya Nair (Redwood): we support customer-managed KMS; keys can be in your cloud account. For on-prem/private we can also integrate HSM. We'll attach standard vendor security docs.
[06:49] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): curious about observability — tokens, cost breakdown, per-route latency, can we surface that in our Datadog?
[06:57] Leo Martinez (Redwood): yes, metrics export available; console has built-in dashboards and you can forward metrics/logs to Datadog/CloudWatch.
[07:05] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): competitor checks — we've seen offerings from Lambda and a few self-hosted toolchains, but their ops overhead is high. We also evaluated Run:ai. What do customers typically say vs those?
[07:16] Jordan Kim (Redwood): customers pick us for the production focus: predictable economics, integrated routing/console, and simpler lifecycle management vs building orchestration yourself. We'll include a competitive sheet.
[07:26] Owen Li (PolarisComms): SLA expectations — what's a realistic SLO for P95 given the mix of pinned micro-models and larger fallback models?
[07:34] Priya Nair (Redwood): with pinned micro-models you can expect ~40-80ms P95 for those flows. Larger gen models will be higher; we calibrate rollouts so user-facing critical paths use pinned models.
[07:47] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): can you run a short benchmark mimicking our 900 RPS 2-min spike to validate?
[07:52] Jordan Kim (Redwood): yes — we'll propose a 24h benchmark window that includes stress spikes. We'll need a test harness from you, and we'll spin a dedicated pilot environment.
[08:02] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): what's the minimum reserved commitment to run a pilot?
[08:07] Jordan Kim (Redwood): pilots can be small — often customers put a modest reserved commit (1-2 GPUs) plus burst credits and warm-pool config; for a faithful stress test we'll size it higher but can do a scoped run. We'll put numbers in the spreadsheet.
[08:20] Samir Vyas (PolarisComms): legal/procurement — data residency is important; certain league data must stay in EU. Do you support regional isolation?
[08:29] Priya Nair (Redwood): yes — region pinning and routing policies by geography. For regulated flows we recommend Dedicated in a region or Private if you need absolute control.
[08:39] Owen Li (PolarisComms): curious about model onboarding — we run a couple internal models and an open-source fine-tuned model. What's the process?
[08:45] Leo Martinez (Redwood): we onboard by taking your artifacts (containerized or model files), run compatibility checks, and recommend quantization profiles. There's a staging verification and a rollout plan with canary traffic. We also do perf profiling to recommend kernel/compilation settings.
[09:02] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): licensing on models — any concerns with redistributing closed models?
[09:07] Priya Nair (Redwood): if it's customer-owned model that stays within their VPC or private deployment, licensing is your responsibility; we support bringing-your-own-model. For hosted models we curate open models and share provenance.
[09:18] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): small nit: you mentioned KV cache earlier as "KV cash" in the docs, haha — we need to confirm how shared the KV cache is across tenants.
[09:26] Leo Martinez (Redwood): ha noted. KV cache is per-tenant by default on Dedicated, and for multi-tenant pods we have fencing. There's an option for shared prefix caches for certain workflows but not for PII.
[09:38] Owen Li (PolarisComms): incident scenarios — if a reserved node fails during kickoff, what's the failover sequence?
[09:45] Priya Nair (Redwood): we have automatic routing to standby capacity; if standby isn't enough we fallback to hosted variants or lower-precision models by policy. We also provide real-time alerts and a runbook.
[09:58] Jordan Kim (Redwood): recap: we need telemetry, model artifacts, security checklist, and a test harness. We'll prepare sizing, pricing, and a security pack; propose a pilot window for Q2.
[10:10] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): sounds good. Quick question on support — what's the support SLA during pilot vs production?
[10:16] Jordan Kim (Redwood): pilots get standard support; enterprise customers with Dedicated get 24/7 support options and escalation. We'll outline tiers.
[10:24] Nora Chen (PolarisComms): and do you provide runbooks for on-call?
[10:28] Leo Martinez (Redwood): yes, we'll hand over runbooks and playbooks for burst scenarios.
[10:33] Samir Vyas (PolarisComms): ok if you send SOC2 and KMS docs asap that helps for procurement review.
[10:39] Jordan Kim (Redwood): will do. Anything else?
[10:42] Maya Patel (PolarisComms): no, that's it. thanks everyone.
[10:45] Jordan Kim (Redwood): thanks all, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and security pack and schedule the benchmark.
[10:50] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: speech disfluencies present; occasional word swaps (KV cash / kv cache), speaker overlap minimal.
